items.stem: A laser beam hits a flat reflecting surface at an angle of incidence of 73°. State the angle between the incident and the reflected beam.
items.markingKey: 146° – angles of incidence and reflection are equal and measured from the normal (A1).

items.stem: Distinguish between reflection and refraction.
items.answer: In reflection the wave returns into the same medium with unchanged speed and wavelength (i = r); in refraction the wave enters a new medium, its speed and wavelength change and (at oblique incidence) its direction changes.
items.markingKey: In reflection the wave returns into the same medium with unchanged speed and wavelength (i = r); in refraction the wave enters a new medium, its speed and wavelength change and (at oblique incidence) its direction changes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Waves bend towards the normal whenever they pass into a denser material." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: What matters is wave speed, not density: sound travels faster in water than in air and so bends away from the normal on entering water.
items.markingKey: What matters is wave speed, not density: sound travels faster in water than in air and so bends away from the normal on entering water. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Light of wavelength 450 nm in a vacuum enters glycerol (refractive index 1.47). What is its wavelength in glycerol?
items.answer: 306 nm
items.markingKey: B. λ = λ₀/n = 450/1.47 = 306 nm; frequency is unchanged so the wavelength falls by the factor n.

items.stem: Mei photographed the shadows of ripple-tank waves and measured them from the photograph. The 5 readings of the distance spanned by ten wavefronts were 14.2, 14.3, 14.3, 14.6, 14.5 cm. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 14.4 cm (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.2 cm (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.2/14.4 × 100 = 1.4 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Water waves of wavelength 3.0 cm travel in deep water at 24 cm s⁻¹ towards a straight boundary with shallow water, where their speed is 16 cm s⁻¹. The wavefronts make 35° with the boundary. (a) State the angle of incidence of the rays. (b) Determine the angle of refraction and the new wavelength. (c) Explain whether the waves could be totally internally reflected if they travelled the other way.
items.answer: (a) 35°; (b) 22.5°, 2.0 cm; (c) yes – going from shallow to deep the waves speed up, so above the critical angle of 41.8° they are totally reflected.
items.markingKey: Angle between wavefront and boundary equals angle between ray and normal = 35° (A1); sin θ₂ = (16/24) sin 35° (M1), θ₂ = 22.5° (A1); λ = 3.0 × 16/24 = 2.0 cm (A1); TIR possible from slow to fast medium, critical angle sin⁻¹(16/24) = 41.8° (R1).

items.stem: A ray meets a boundary along the normal. What happens to the transmitted ray?
options: It is bent towards the normal.
It continues without a change of direction but with a change of speed.
items.answer: It continues without a change of direction but with a change of speed.
items.markingKey: C. At normal incidence sin θ₁ = 0, so θ₂ = 0: speed and wavelength change but direction does not.

items.stem: Explain, using wavefronts, why a wave bends towards the normal when it enters a medium in which it travels more slowly.
items.answer: The part of an oblique wavefront that reaches the boundary first slows down while the rest continues at the higher speed; the wavefront swings round so that it travels closer to the normal.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The part of an oblique wavefront that reaches the boundary first slows down while the rest continues at the higher speed; the wavefront swings round so that it travels closer to the normal. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ocean swell of frequency 0.100 Hz travels at 9.00 m s⁻¹ in the open ocean. Calculate its wavelength in the open ocean.

A student investigates water waves in a ripple tank of constant depth. The dipper frequency f is varied and the wavelength λ is measured with a stroboscope. Theory predicts λ = v/f.

f / Hz | λ / cm
4.0 | 6.36
6.0 | 4.33
8.0 | 3.19
10.0 | 2.67
12.0 | 2.12

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the speed of the waves. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State the wave speed with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) λ against 1/f (λ in m); (b) gradient ≈ 0.252 m s⁻¹; (c) 0.252 m s⁻¹; (d) 0.252 m s⁻¹ ± 0.01 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) λ against 1/f (λ in m) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 0.252 m s⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) v = gradient = 0.252 m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 0.01 m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: "The ray model of light is sufficient to explain all optical phenomena." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The ray model is a useful simplification valid when apertures are much larger than the wavelength; a complete account needs wave and photon models – an example of models having limited domains of validity (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rays predict reflection, refraction and image formation accurately; ray diagrams are simple and useful for lens and mirror design. Arguments against: rays cannot explain diffraction or interference, which need a wave (wavefront) model; polarisation and the photoelectric effect need wave and photon models respectively. Supported judgement: The ray model is a useful simplification valid when apertures are much larger than the wavelength; a complete account needs wave and photon models – an example of models having limited domains of validity (NOS). Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "total internal reflection"?
options: Complete reflection of a wave at a boundary with a medium of lower refractive index when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
The distance between the centres of adjacent bright (or dark) fringes, s = λD/d in a double-slit pattern
N₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for a ray crossing a boundary between media of refractive indices n₁ and n₂
The spreading of a wave as it passes through an aperture or around an obstacle
items.answer: Complete reflection of a wave at a boundary with a medium of lower refractive index when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
items.markingKey: A. "total internal reflection" is complete reflection of a wave at a boundary with a medium of lower refractive index when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

items.stem: Explain the difference between partial reflection and total internal reflection.
items.answer: Partial reflection happens at any boundary with some light also refracted; total internal reflection happens only for light going into a lower-index medium above the critical angle, when no light is refracted.
items.markingKey: Partial reflection happens at any boundary with some light also refracted; total internal reflection happens only for light going into a lower-index medium above the critical angle, when no light is refracted. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Zara writes four statements while revising Snell's law, refractive index and critical angle. Which one is a misconception?
options: The frequency stays constant; it is the wavelength that decreases (λ = v/f) because the speed decreases.
Grating angles are large, so the exact relation n λ = d sin θ must be used.
Superposition is temporary: after crossing, each wave continues unchanged; energy is redistributed, not destroyed.
At the critical angle all the light is totally internally reflected.
items.answer: At the critical angle all the light is totally internally reflected.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: At exactly the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface (90°); total internal reflection occurs only for angles of incidence greater than the critical angle.

items.stem: A student claims: "At the critical angle all the light is totally internally reflected." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: At exactly the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface (90°); total internal reflection occurs only for angles of incidence greater than the critical angle.
items.markingKey: At exactly the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface (90°); total internal reflection occurs only for angles of incidence greater than the critical angle. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Light travels in water (n = 1.33) and meets a boundary with ice (n = 1.31) at an angle of incidence of 33°. Calculate the angle of refraction in ice.
What is the critical angle for light in ethanol (n = 1.36) at a boundary with air?
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Optical fibres have completely replaced copper cables for communication."
items.answer: Fibres dominate long-distance and high-bandwidth links, but copper remains common for short connections and power, so "completely replaced" overstates the case.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fibres carry far higher bandwidth with low attenuation; immune to electromagnetic interference and harder to tap; lighter and cheaper per bit over long distances. Arguments against: copper is still used for the "last mile", power supply and short links; fibres need precise splicing and optical-electrical conversion; dispersion and attenuation still limit range without repeaters. Supported judgement: Fibres dominate long-distance and high-bandwidth links, but copper remains common for short connections and power, so "completely replaced" overstates the case.

items.stem: A right-angled isosceles glass prism (angles 45°, 45°, 90°) is used in binoculars to turn light through 180°. (a) Determine the minimum refractive index of the glass for the light to be totally internally reflected at each hypotenuse face. (b) Explain why prisms are preferred to silvered mirrors in high-quality instruments. (c) Discuss what would happen if the prism were immersed in water (n = 1.33) and its index were 1.52.
items.answer: (a) n ≥ 1/sin 45° = 1.41; (b) TIR reflects almost 100 % with no tarnishing or double images; (c) critical angle becomes sin⁻¹(1.33/1.52) = 61°, so 45° incidence no longer gives TIR – light escapes into the water.
items.markingKey: Angle of incidence at the face is 45° (M1); n sin 45° ≥ 1 → n ≥ 1.41 (A1); TIR loses no energy, no coating to degrade (R1); new critical angle 61° calculated (M1); 45° < 61°, so TIR fails (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Complete reflection of a wave at a boundary with a medium of lower refractive index when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle"?
items.answer: total internal reflection
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of total internal reflection.

items.stem: The critical angle for a glass–air boundary is 42°. If the glass is placed in water instead of air, the critical angle
items.answer: increases
items.markingKey: C. sin c = n_water/n_glass is larger than 1/n_glass, so c increases.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a ray entering a glass block along the normal is not deviated.
items.answer: For θ₁ = 0, Snell’s law gives sin θ₂ = 0, so θ₂ = 0; the wavefronts are parallel to the boundary and all parts slow down at the same time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: For θ₁ = 0, Snell’s law gives sin θ₂ = 0, so θ₂ = 0; the wavefronts are parallel to the boundary and all parts slow down at the same time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A ray travelling inside quartz (n = 1.54) meets the boundary with air (n = 1.0) at an angle of incidence of 37°. Determine whether the ray is totally internally reflected, and justify your answer with a calculation.
items.answer: critical angle 40.5°; the ray is refracted out, at 67.9°
items.markingKey: sin c = 1.0/1.54 (M1), c = 40.5° (A1); 37° < c so the ray refracts out (some partial reflection) (R1).

items.stem:
In an experiment to find the refractive index of a glass block, the angle of incidence θ₁ in air and angle of refraction θ₂ in the glass were measured with a protractor (uncertainty ±1°).

θ₁ / ° | θ₂ / °
10 | 7
20 | 14
30 | 20
40 | 26
50 | 31
60 | 37

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the refractive index of the glass. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State the refractive index with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) sin θ₂ (y) against sin θ₁ (x); (b) gradient ≈ 0.679 ; (c) 1.47; (d) 1.47 ± 0.03
items.markingKey: (a) sin θ₂ (y) against sin θ₁ (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 0.679  – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) n = 1/gradient = 1.47 (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 0.03 ; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A step-index optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.467 and cladding of refractive index 1.446. (a) Calculate the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary. (b) Show that the maximum angle of incidence in air at the end of the fibre for which light is guided is about 14°. (c) The fibre is 2.0 km long. Calculate the difference in travel time between a ray along the axis and a ray at the critical angle, and explain why this limits the data rate.
items.answer: (a) 80.3°; (b) 14.3°; (c) 1.42 × 10⁻⁷ s – pulses spread out (multipath dispersion) and overlap if sent too frequently
items.markingKey: (a) sin c = 1.446/1.467, c = 80.3° (M1 A1). (b) Angle in core at entry = 90° − c (M1); sin θₐ = 1.467 sin(90° − c) = √(n₁² − n₂²) (M1), θₐ = 14.3° (A1). (c) axial t = n₁L/c = 9.78 × 10⁻⁶ s; critical ray path longer by n₁/n₂: t = 9.92 × 10⁻⁶ s (M1); Δt = 1.42 × 10⁻⁷ s (A1); pulse broadening → pulses must be separated by more than Δt (R1).

items.stem: Two waves of amplitude 3 cm and 5 cm meet in antiphase. What is the resultant amplitude?
items.answer: 2 cm
items.markingKey: 2 cm (A1). Antiphase: 5 − 3 = 2 cm.

items.stem: Explain whether the waves spread out more or less after the gap when a loudspeaker playing a low note of 200 Hz is replaced by a whistle at 4000 Hz in the same doorway.
items.answer: The waves spread less after the gap, because the 4000 Hz sound has a wavelength of about 8.5 cm, much smaller than the doorway, compared with 1.7 m at 200 Hz.
items.markingKey: Spreading less (A1); because the 4000 Hz sound has a wavelength of about 8.5 cm, much smaller than the doorway, compared with 1.7 m at 200 Hz – diffraction depends on λ/gap (R1).

items.stem: Distinguish between constructive interference and destructive interference.
items.answer: Constructive: waves arrive in phase (path difference nλ) and amplitudes add; destructive: waves arrive in antiphase (path difference (n + ½)λ) and amplitudes subtract.
items.markingKey: Constructive: waves arrive in phase (path difference nλ) and amplitudes add; destructive: waves arrive in antiphase (path difference (n + ½)λ) and amplitudes subtract. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Two coherent sources emit waves in phase with wavelength 0.80 m. At point P the path difference is 0.200 m. Calculate the phase difference at P (in radians) and state the type of interference.
items.answer: 1.57 rad (90.0°); neither fully constructive nor destructive
items.markingKey: φ = 2πΔx/λ = 2π × 0.200/0.80 (M1) = 1.57 rad (A1); neither fully constructive nor destructive (R1).

items.stem: "Interference only happens with light." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Interference is a property of all waves – sound, water waves, microwaves and matter waves (electrons) all show it.
items.markingKey: Interference is a property of all waves – sound, water waves, microwaves and matter waves (electrons) all show it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two coherent sources S₁ and S₂ in a ripple tank are 6.0 cm apart and vibrate in phase at 12 Hz; the wave speed is 0.18 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Point P is 10.5 cm from S₁ and 13.5 cm from S₂: determine the type of interference at P. (c) Describe how the pattern changes if the two dippers vibrate in antiphase.
items.answer: (a) λ = 0.18/12 = 1.5 cm; (b) path difference 3.0 cm = 2λ → constructive (antinodal line); (c) all maxima and minima swap: P becomes a point of destructive interference and the central line becomes a nodal line.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = 0.18/12 = 1.5 cm; (b) path difference 3.0 cm = 2λ → constructive (antinodal line); (c) all maxima and minima swap: P becomes a point of destructive interference and the central line becomes a nodal line.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "diffraction"?
options: The ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the speed of light in the medium, n = c/v
The angle θ = λ/b at which waves from the two halves of a slit of width b cancel
The spreading of a wave as it passes through an aperture or around an obstacle
A line showing the direction in which a wave transfers energy; it is perpendicular to the wavefronts
items.answer: The spreading of a wave as it passes through an aperture or around an obstacle
items.markingKey: C. "diffraction" is the spreading of a wave as it passes through an aperture or around an obstacle.

items.stem: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator produce a pattern of loud and quiet regions. If the generator frequency is doubled, the spacing between loud regions
items.answer: roughly halves
items.markingKey: D. λ halves, so the positions where path difference = nλ move closer together.

items.stem: Two coherent waves of wavelength 2.0 cm, emitted in phase, meet with a path difference of 1.50 cm. What is their phase difference (between 0° and 360°)?
items.markingKey: D. Phase difference = 360° × Δx/λ = 360° × 0.75 = 270°, i.e. 270° within one cycle.

items.stem: Two coherent sources emit waves in phase with wavelength 0.80 m. At point P the path difference is 2.00 m. Calculate the phase difference at P (in radians) and state the type of interference.
items.answer: 15.7 rad (900°); destructive
items.markingKey: φ = 2πΔx/λ = 2π × 2.00/0.80 (M1) = 15.7 rad (A1); destructive (R1).

items.stem: "Young’s observation of interference proved that light is a wave." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Interference was strong evidence for wave behaviour, but modern physics treats light with wave–particle duality; scientific evidence supports rather than proves models.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: interference fringes are explained naturally by superposition of waves; the corpuscular model could not explain dark fringes. Arguments against: the photoelectric effect later required a particle (photon) model; single photons still build up an interference pattern, so the wave picture alone is incomplete; evidence supports but never "proves" a theory (NOS). Supported judgement: Interference was strong evidence for wave behaviour, but modern physics treats light with wave–particle duality; scientific evidence supports rather than proves models. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to a point"?
items.answer: path difference
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of path difference.

items.stem: Explain why the light from the two slits in Young’s experiment is coherent.
items.answer: Both slits are illuminated by the same wavefront from a single (laser or slit) source, so the light leaving them has the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both slits are illuminated by the same wavefront from a single (laser or slit) source, so the light leaving them has the same frequency and a constant phase difference. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In a Young’s double-slit experiment, state and explain the effect on the fringe spacing when the slits are made narrower but kept the same distance apart.
items.answer: The fringe spacing is unchanged, but the pattern becomes dimmer and the fringes extend over a wider region; narrower slits diffract more, widening the single-slit envelope.
items.markingKey: Effect: spacing is unchanged, but the pattern becomes dimmer and the fringes extend over a wider region (A1); reason: narrower slits diffract more, widening the single-slit envelope (R1).

items.stem: Noah writes: "Bright fringes occur where the path difference is λ/2." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Bright fringes need path difference nλ (whole wavelengths); λ/2 gives a dark fringe.
items.markingKey: Bright fringes need path difference nλ (whole wavelengths); λ/2 gives a dark fringe. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Light from a red laser of wavelength 633 nm illuminates two slits 0.30 mm apart. The screen is 2.00 m away. Calculate the fringe spacing.
Monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.25 mm apart. What is the fringe separation on a screen 1.6 m away?

A student measures the wavelength of a laser with a double slit. Data: distance across 10 fringe spacings x = (62 ± 1) mm; slit-to-screen distance D = (2.46 ± 0.01) m; slit separation d = (0.25 ± 0.01) mm.

(a) Calculate the wavelength. [2]
(b) Determine the percentage uncertainty in the wavelength. [2]
(c) Identify which measurement contributes most to the uncertainty and suggest one improvement. [1]
items.answer: (a) λ = 630 nm; (b) 6.0 %; (c) d – measure d with a travelling microscope or use a slit pair with a larger, better-known separation
items.markingKey: (a) s = x/10 = 6.2 mm (M1); λ = sd/D = 630 nm (A1). (b) %Δλ = %Δx + %ΔD + %Δd = 1.6 + 0.4 + 4.0 (M1) = 6.0 % (A1). (c) largest contribution from d; measure d with a travelling microscope or use a slit pair with a larger, better-known separation (A1).

items.stem: "Young’s double-slit experiment was immediately accepted as decisive evidence against Newton’s corpuscular theory." Discuss.
items.answer: It became decisive only over time, after further theory and experiments; scientific acceptance is a community process.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gave a clear wave explanation of fringes and measured wavelengths. Arguments against: Newton’s authority meant many resisted Young’s ideas for years; acceptance grew only after Fresnel’s mathematical theory and Arago’s spot; social and authority factors influence acceptance (NOS). Supported judgement: It became decisive only over time, after further theory and experiments; scientific acceptance is a community process. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: A student in Dubai is checking notes on double-slit interference and path difference. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are measured from the normal, not from the surface.
Increasing the slit separation spreads the fringes further apart.
Superposition is temporary: after crossing, each wave continues unchanged; energy is redistributed, not destroyed.
It is the ratio of the sines that is constant: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂; θ₁/θ₂ is not constant except approximately at small angles.
items.answer: Increasing the slit separation spreads the fringes further apart.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: s = λD/d: increasing d makes the fringes closer together.

items.stem: In a double-slit experiment the third bright fringe from the centre is at point P. What is the path difference to P?
items.answer: 3λ
items.markingKey: C. nth bright fringe: path difference nλ with n = 3.

items.stem: Distinguish between a double-slit pattern and a single-slit pattern.
items.answer: A double-slit pattern has equally spaced fringes of (nearly) equal width from interference of two coherent sources; a single-slit pattern has a central maximum twice as wide as the others and intensity falling rapidly outwards, from diffraction across one slit.
items.markingKey: A double-slit pattern has equally spaced fringes of (nearly) equal width from interference of two coherent sources; a single-slit pattern has a central maximum twice as wide as the others and intensity falling rapidly outwards, from diffraction across one slit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Two loudspeakers driven in phase emit sound of frequency 1360 Hz (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). Diego stands 4.83 m from one speaker and 5.705 m from the other. Determine whether Diego hears a loud or a quiet sound.
items.answer: path difference = 0.875 m = 3.5λ, so quiet (destructive)
items.markingKey: λ = 340/1360 = 0.25 m (A1); path difference = 0.875 m (M1); = 3.5λ, odd multiple of λ/2 → destructive (R1).

items.stem: Two radio transmitters 300 m apart broadcast the same 1.0 MHz signal in phase. A car drives along a road parallel to the line joining them, 5.0 km away. (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Determine the distance between positions of minimum signal along the road. (c) Explain why the minima are not of zero signal.
items.answer: (a) λ = c/f = 300 m; (b) s = λD/d = 300 × 5000/300 = 5.0 km (small-angle approximation only roughly valid); (c) the two signals arrive with unequal amplitudes (different distances, ground reflections), so cancellation is incomplete.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = c/f = 300 m; (b) s = λD/d = 300 × 5000/300 = 5.0 km (small-angle approximation only roughly valid); (c) the two signals arrive with unequal amplitudes (different distances, ground reflections), so cancellation is incomplete.

items.stem:
A student measures the wavelength of a laser with a double slit. Data: distance across 10 fringe spacings x = (43 ± 1) mm; slit-to-screen distance D = (1.66 ± 0.01) m; slit separation d = (0.25 ± 0.01) mm.

(a) Calculate the wavelength. [2]
(b) Determine the percentage uncertainty in the wavelength. [2]
(c) Identify which measurement contributes most to the uncertainty and suggest one improvement. [1]
items.answer: (a) λ = 648 nm; (b) 6.9 %; (c) d – measure d with a travelling microscope or use a slit pair with a larger, better-known separation
items.markingKey: (a) s = x/10 = 4.3 mm (M1); λ = sd/D = 648 nm (A1). (b) %Δλ = %Δx + %ΔD + %Δd = 2.3 + 0.6 + 4.0 (M1) = 6.9 % (A1). (c) largest contribution from d; measure d with a travelling microscope or use a slit pair with a larger, better-known separation (A1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The distance between adjacent slits of a grating, d = 1/N where N is the number of lines per metre"?
items.answer: grating spacing
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of grating spacing.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a single-slit diffraction pattern and a diffraction grating pattern.
items.answer: A single slit gives a broad central maximum (width 2λ/b) and weak subsidiary maxima; a grating gives very sharp, bright principal maxima at angles where d sin θ = nλ with darkness in between.
items.markingKey: A single slit gives a broad central maximum (width 2λ/b) and weak subsidiary maxima; a grating gives very sharp, bright principal maxima at angles where d sin θ = nλ with darkness in between. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The number of lines per mm of a grating is doubled. The angle of the first-order maximum
items.answer: increases, with sin θ doubling
items.markingKey: A. d halves so sin θ = λ/d doubles (the angle itself less than doubles).

items.stem: The first-order maximum for a spectral line seen through a 100 lines per mm grating is at 3.63°. Calculate the wavelength of the line.
items.answer: 633 nm

items.stem:
A student shines a laser normally onto gratings with different numbers of lines per mm, N, and measures the angle θ of the first-order maximum. Theory: sin θ = λN.

N / lines mm⁻¹ | θ / °
100 | 3.3
200 | 6.9
300 | 10.1
400 | 13.8
500 | 17.1
600 | 20.8

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the wavelength of the laser. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±5 %. State the wavelength with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) sin θ (y) against N (in lines per metre); (b) gradient ≈ 5.92 × 10⁻⁷ m; (c) 592 nm; (d) 592 nm ± 30 nm
items.markingKey: (a) sin θ (y) against N (in lines per metre) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 5.92 × 10⁻⁷ m – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) λ = gradient = 592 nm (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 5 % of the value = 30 nm; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A double slit has slit width b = 0.050 mm and slit separation d = 0.20 mm and is lit with 532 nm laser light. (a) Calculate the angle of the first single-slit minimum. (b) Determine how many bright interference fringes lie within the central diffraction maximum. (c) Explain why the order-4 fringe is missing.
items.answer: (a) 0.0106 rad (0.610°); (b) 7; (c) the order-4 maximum (d sin θ = 4λ) falls at the same angle as the first single-slit minimum (b sin θ = λ)
items.markingKey: (a) θ = λ/b (M1) = 0.0106 rad (A1). (b) d/b = 4, so orders −3 … +3: 7 fringes (M1 A1). (c) at sin θ = λ/b = 4λ/d the envelope is zero, so the interference maximum has zero intensity (R1).

items.stem: In a double-slit pattern observed carefully, the intensity of the interference fringes varies because
options: the wavelength changes across the screen
it is modulated by the single-slit diffraction envelope of each slit
items.answer: it is modulated by the single-slit diffraction envelope of each slit
items.markingKey: D. Each slit has finite width, so the fringes lie under a diffraction envelope.

items.stem: Explain why there is a maximum number of orders produced by a grating.
items.answer: sin θ cannot exceed 1, so n ≤ d/λ; the highest order is the largest integer below d/λ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: sin θ cannot exceed 1, so n ≤ d/λ; the highest order is the largest integer below d/λ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm is incident normally on a grating with 600 lines per mm. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
"The small-angle formula s = λD/d is used to find the angles from a diffraction grating." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Grating angles are large, so the exact relation n λ = d sin θ must be used.
items.markingKey: Grating angles are large, so the exact relation n λ = d sin θ must be used. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Define the term "total internal reflection".
items.answer: Complete reflection of a wave at a boundary with a medium of lower refractive index when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: complete reflection of a wave at a boundary with a medium of lower refractive index when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: For a dark fringe in a two-source interference pattern (sources in phase), the path difference is
items.answer: (n + ½)λ
items.markingKey: A. Antiphase arrival requires a half-wavelength odd multiple.

items.stem: Define the term "wavefront".
items.answer: A line or surface joining neighbouring points on a wave that oscillate in phase
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a line or surface joining neighbouring points on a wave that oscillate in phase. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Mei is revising diffraction and the principle of superposition. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Superposition is temporary: after crossing, each wave continues unchanged; energy is redistributed, not destroyed.
Bright fringes occur where the path difference is λ/2.
A narrower gap always gives less diffraction.
Increasing the slit separation spreads the fringes further apart.
items.answer: Superposition is temporary: after crossing, each wave continues unchanged; energy is redistributed, not destroyed.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. Superposition is temporary: after crossing, each wave continues unchanged; energy is redistributed, not destroyed.

items.stem: Alessia and a classmate in Seoul disagree about single-slit diffraction and diffraction gratings (HL). Which statement is correct?
options: Θ = λ/b: a wider slit gives a narrower central maximum.
The angle of incidence is measured between the ray and the surface.
Increasing the slit separation spreads the fringes further apart.
The small-angle formula s = λD/d is used to find the angles from a diffraction grating.
items.answer: Θ = λ/b: a wider slit gives a narrower central maximum.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. Θ = λ/b: a wider slit gives a narrower central maximum.

items.stem: Outline how the data from an experiment testing n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for light entering a glass block from air should be linearised, and state the features of the graph that would confirm the relationship.
items.answer: Plot sin θ₁ (y-axis) against sin θ₂ (x-axis); gradient = the refractive index of the glass. A straight line through the origin confirms Snell’s law.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: sin θ₁ against sin θ₂ (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = the refractive index of the glass (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms Snell’s law.

items.stem: In a Young’s double-slit experiment, state and explain the effect on the fringe spacing when blue light replaces red light.
items.answer: The fringe spacing decreases; s ∝ λ and blue light has a shorter wavelength.
items.markingKey: Effect: spacing decreases (A1); reason: s ∝ λ and blue light has a shorter wavelength (R1).

items.stem: Plane waves travelling at speed v cross into a region where they travel at v/2. The angle of incidence is 0°. Which describes the transmitted waves?
options: bent towards the normal, half the wavelength
items.answer: same direction, half the wavelength
items.markingKey: B. At normal incidence there is no change in direction; f is unchanged so λ halves.

items.stem: Explain why energy is conserved in an interference pattern even though there are points of zero intensity.
items.answer: Energy is redistributed: intensity missing from minima appears at maxima (where intensity ∝ (2A)² = 4A²), so the average intensity is unchanged.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Energy is redistributed: intensity missing from minima appears at maxima (where intensity ∝ (2A)² = 4A²), so the average intensity is unchanged. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A diffraction grating has 600 lines per mm. Determine the highest order maximum that can be observed for light of wavelength 633 nm.
items.markingKey: d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m; n ≤ d/λ = 2.63 (M1); highest whole order n = 2 (A1).

items.stem: Light in air is incident at 45° to the normal on a flat surface of flint glass of refractive index 1.62. What is the angle of refraction?
items.markingKey: D. sin θ₂ = sin 45°/1.62; θ₂ = 25.9°. Dividing the angle itself by n, or measuring from the surface, gives the distractors.

items.stem: In a double-slit experiment with slit separation 0.50 mm and screen distance 1.50 m, 9 consecutive bright fringes span 9.72 mm. Determine the wavelength of the light.
items.answer: 405 nm
items.markingKey: 9 bright fringes = 8 spacings, s = 9.72/8 mm (M1); λ = sd/D (M1) = 405 nm (A1).

items.stem: Mei used a stroboscope to freeze the waves in a ripple tank and measured the waves on a ruler on the screen. The 5 readings of the distance spanned by ten wavefronts were 13.7, 13.8, 14.5, 13.7, 14.5 cm. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 14.0 cm (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.4 cm (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.4/14.0 × 100 = 2.8 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: Maya shone a laser through an adjustable slit and measured the pattern on a screen. The 5 readings of the angular width of the central diffraction maximum were 6.0, 5.9, 6.3, 6.1, 6.0 °. Determine the mean, the absolute uncertainty and the percentage uncertainty, and state the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
items.markingKey: Mean = 6.1 ° (A1); absolute uncertainty = half range = 0.2 ° (A1); percentage uncertainty = 0.2/6.1 × 100 = 3.3 % (A1). Result quoted to the same decimal place as the uncertainty.

items.stem: "A wider slit gives a wider central diffraction maximum." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: θ = λ/b: a wider slit gives a narrower central maximum.
items.markingKey: θ = λ/b: a wider slit gives a narrower central maximum. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A ray travelling inside ice (n = 1.31) meets the boundary with air (n = 1.0) at an angle of incidence of 43°. Determine whether the ray is totally internally reflected, and justify your answer with a calculation.
items.answer: critical angle 49.8°; the ray is refracted out, at 63.3°
items.markingKey: sin c = 1.0/1.31 (M1), c = 49.8° (A1); 43° < c so the ray refracts out (some partial reflection) (R1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Young’s double-slit experiment was immediately accepted as decisive evidence against Newton’s corpuscular theory."
items.answer: It became decisive only over time, after further theory and experiments; scientific acceptance is a community process.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gave a clear wave explanation of fringes and measured wavelengths. Arguments against: Newton’s authority meant many resisted Young’s ideas for years; acceptance grew only after Fresnel’s mathematical theory and Arago’s spot; social and authority factors influence acceptance (NOS). Supported judgement: It became decisive only over time, after further theory and experiments; scientific acceptance is a community process.

items.stem: A plane water wave of frequency 5.0 Hz travels at 0.30 m s⁻¹ in deep water and meets a straight boundary with shallow water at an angle of incidence of 40°. In the shallow water its speed is 0.20 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the wavelength in each region. (b) Calculate the angle of refraction. (c) Sketch and describe the wavefronts in both regions.
items.answer: (a) 6.0 cm in deep water and 4.0 cm in shallow water; (b) sin θ₂ = (0.20/0.30) sin 40° → θ₂ = 25.4°; (c) wavefronts closer together in the shallow region and turned towards the boundary, rays bent towards the normal.
items.markingKey: (a) 6.0 cm in deep water and 4.0 cm in shallow water; (b) sin θ₂ = (0.20/0.30) sin 40° → θ₂ = 25.4°; (c) wavefronts closer together in the shallow region and turned towards the boundary, rays bent towards the normal.

items.stem: Noise-cancelling headphones use a microphone to detect ambient sound and emit a sound wave to cancel it. Discuss the physics of this method and explain why it works better for low-frequency engine hum than for high-frequency speech.
items.answer: The headphone produces a wave of equal amplitude in antiphase with the incoming sound, so superposition gives near-zero resultant displacement at the ear. For low frequencies the wavelength is long and the waveform changes slowly, so small time delays or position differences cause only small phase errors; at high frequencies, wavelengths are short (a few cm) and processing delays produce large phase errors, so cancellation fails.
items.markingKey: Antiphase wave of equal amplitude (M1); superposition gives destructive interference (R1); requires coherent (matched) signal, continuous processing (R1); phase error = 2πΔt·f grows with frequency (R1); conclusion supported (A1).

items.stem: The sodium "D lines" have wavelengths 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm. Light from a sodium lamp falls normally on a grating with 500 lines per mm. (a) Calculate the angle of each line in order 1. (b) Determine their angular separation. (c) Explain why a grating with more lines illuminated, rather than a double slit, is needed to see the two lines separately.
items.answer: (a) 17.128° and 17.146°; (b) 0.018°; (c) many slits make each maximum very narrow so the two close maxima do not overlap
items.markingKey: d = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m (A1); sin θ = nλ/d for each (M1), θ = 17.128° and 17.146° (A1); Δθ = 0.018° (A1); grating maxima narrower than the separation, double-slit fringes far too broad (R1 R1).

items.stem: In an optical fibre, why is the core given a higher refractive index than the cladding?
options: so that the cladding absorbs stray light
so that light refracts out of the fibre
so that light can be totally internally reflected at the core–cladding boundary
so that light travels faster in the core
items.answer: so that light can be totally internally reflected at the core–cladding boundary
items.markingKey: C. TIR only occurs going from higher to lower refractive index.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "path difference".
items.answer: The difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to a point
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the difference in the distances travelled by two waves from their sources to a point. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ray"?
options: Superposition of waves arriving in antiphase, giving a resultant amplitude equal to the difference of the amplitudes
N₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for a ray crossing a boundary between media of refractive indices n₁ and n₂
The integer n such that the path difference to the fringe is nλ for a bright fringe
A line showing the direction in which a wave transfers energy; it is perpendicular to the wavefronts
items.answer: A line showing the direction in which a wave transfers energy; it is perpendicular to the wavefronts
items.markingKey: D. "ray" is a line showing the direction in which a wave transfers energy; it is perpendicular to the wavefronts.

items.stem: Distinguish between diffraction and refraction.
items.answer: Diffraction is spreading at an aperture or edge in the same medium, with no change of speed; refraction is a change of direction caused by a change of speed at a boundary between media.
items.markingKey: Diffraction is spreading at an aperture or edge in the same medium, with no change of speed; refraction is a change of direction caused by a change of speed at a boundary between media. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ana and a classmate in Vienna disagree about single-slit diffraction and diffraction gratings (HL). Which statement is correct?
options: The angle of incidence is measured between the ray and the surface.
Bright fringes occur where the path difference is λ/2.
Two waves that superpose destructively destroy each other’s energy permanently.
Grating angles are large, so the exact relation n λ = d sin θ must be used.
items.answer: Grating angles are large, so the exact relation n λ = d sin θ must be used.
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. Grating angles are large, so the exact relation n λ = d sin θ must be used.

items.stem: Light passes from glass (n = 1.5) into water (n = 1.33). Which statement is correct?
options: The light slows down and bends towards the normal.
The light speeds up and bends towards the normal.
The frequency of the light increases.
The light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
items.answer: The light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
items.markingKey: D. Lower refractive index → higher speed → bends away from the normal.

items.stem: Distinguish between path difference and phase difference.
items.answer: Path difference is a distance (in m) between the routes of two waves; phase difference is the corresponding fraction of a cycle, φ = 2πΔx/λ (in rad).
items.markingKey: Path difference is a distance (in m) between the routes of two waves; phase difference is the corresponding fraction of a cycle, φ = 2πΔx/λ (in rad). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame writes four statements while revising wavefronts and rays; reflection and refraction. Which one is a misconception?
options: A wave always changes direction when it crosses a boundary.
Superposition is temporary: after crossing, each wave continues unchanged; energy is redistributed, not destroyed.
Angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are measured from the normal, not from the surface.
More lines per mm means smaller d, so sin θ = nλ/d is larger: maxima at larger angles.
items.answer: A wave always changes direction when it crosses a boundary.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: At normal incidence (along the normal) the wave changes speed and wavelength but not direction.

items.stem: Which observation is evidence for the wave nature of a beam?
options: it produces a diffraction pattern after passing through a narrow gap
it can be reflected from a mirror
items.answer: it produces a diffraction pattern after passing through a narrow gap
items.markingKey: A. Diffraction and interference are characteristic wave behaviours.

items.stem: Light of wavelength 450 nm is incident normally on a grating with 600 lines per mm. At what angle is the first-order maximum?
The speed of light in perspex (acrylic) is 2.01 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. A ray in air enters it at 49° to the normal. Determine the angle of refraction.
A student claims: "Two separate lasers of the same colour will give stable Young’s fringes." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Two independent lasers are not phase-locked; their phase difference drifts, so stable fringes are not normally observed.
items.markingKey: Two independent lasers are not phase-locked; their phase difference drifts, so stable fringes are not normally observed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Light of wavelength 405 nm in a vacuum enters sapphire (refractive index 1.77). What is its wavelength in sapphire?
items.answer: 229 nm
items.markingKey: C. λ = λ₀/n = 405/1.77 = 229 nm; frequency is unchanged so the wavelength falls by the factor n.

items.stem: A student claims: "A narrower gap always gives less diffraction." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A narrower gap (closer to λ) gives MORE spreading; only very wide gaps compared with λ give little diffraction.
items.markingKey: A narrower gap (closer to λ) gives MORE spreading; only very wide gaps compared with λ give little diffraction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A student shines a laser normally onto gratings with different numbers of lines per mm, N, and measures the angle θ of the first-order maximum. Theory: sin θ = λN.

N / lines mm⁻¹ | θ / °
100 | 3.5
200 | 7.1
300 | 11.0
400 | 14.8
500 | 18.5
600 | 22.4

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the wavelength of the laser. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State the wavelength with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) sin θ (y) against N (in lines per metre); (b) gradient ≈ 6.42 × 10⁻⁷ m; (c) 642 nm; (d) 642 nm ± 30 nm
items.markingKey: (a) sin θ (y) against N (in lines per metre) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 6.42 × 10⁻⁷ m – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) λ = gradient = 642 nm (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 30 nm; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Light in air is incident at 60° to the normal on a flat surface of glycerol of refractive index 1.47. What is the angle of refraction?
items.markingKey: D. sin θ₂ = sin 60°/1.47; θ₂ = 36.1°. Dividing the angle itself by n, or measuring from the surface, gives the distractors.

items.stem: A student shines a 650 nm laser through a double slit (d = 0.25 mm) onto a wall 3.20 m away and measures the distance across 10 fringe spacings as 8.3 cm. (a) Determine the wavelength from the data and compare it with 650 nm. (b) Identify two systematic errors that could explain the difference. (c) Explain why the outer fringes appear dimmer.
items.answer: (a) s = 8.3 mm, λ = sd/D = 648 nm, within 0.3 % of 650 nm; (b) slit separation not exactly as labelled, D measured to the wrong point, wall not perpendicular; (c) the pattern is modulated by the single-slit diffraction envelope, which falls off with angle.
items.markingKey: (a) s = 8.3 mm, λ = sd/D = 648 nm, within 0.3 % of 650 nm; (b) slit separation not exactly as labelled, D measured to the wrong point, wall not perpendicular; (c) the pattern is modulated by the single-slit diffraction envelope, which falls off with angle.

items.stem: An engineer models how ocean waves approaching a beach at an angle become almost parallel to the shoreline. Using the idea of wave speed decreasing with depth, explain this observation and suggest why headlands receive more wave energy than bays.
items.answer: As the water gets shallower the wave slows, so the part of each wavefront in shallower water lags behind and the wavefronts turn until they are nearly parallel to the depth contours (the shoreline). Near a headland the depth contours curve round the headland, so refraction concentrates (converges) rays on the headland and spreads (diverges) them in bays.
items.markingKey: Speed decreases with depth (M1); wavefronts turn towards the depth contours / rays turn towards the normal (R1); waves arrive nearly parallel to the shore (A1); convergence of rays on headlands, divergence in bays (R1); link to energy concentration and erosion (A1).

items.stem: Two loudspeakers, 1.5 m apart, are driven in phase at 680 Hz (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). A student walks along a line parallel to the speakers 4.0 m away. (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) Explain why the sound intensity rises and falls. (c) Explain why the minima are not completely silent in a real classroom.
items.answer: (a) 0.50 m; (b) the path difference to the two speakers changes along the line; where it equals nλ there is constructive interference (loud), where (n + ½)λ destructive (quiet); (c) reflections from walls, unequal distances so unequal amplitudes, and background noise.
items.markingKey: λ = v/f = 0.50 m (A1); path difference varies (R1); nλ loud, (n + ½)λ quiet (R1); amplitudes at the minimum are unequal because distances differ (R1); reflections/background noise (R1).

items.stem: "Gratings with as many lines per millimetre as possible are always best for a spectrometer." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Higher line density helps resolution, but the optimum depends on the wavelength range and number of orders required.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smaller d spreads the spectrum over larger angles, improving angular resolution; more illuminated lines give sharper maxima. Arguments against: fewer orders are available (n ≤ d/λ); high orders may be lost entirely and the spectrum may not fit the instrument; manufacturing cost. Supported judgement: Higher line density helps resolution, but the optimum depends on the wavelength range and number of orders required. Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
